transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Patel. Thank you for meeting with me again. I have the answers to the questions you asked during our last visit.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hope you actually have them. I've been thinking about this all week.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I do. To be completely clear about what happened, we gave you a contrast dye for your imaging when your creatinine levels—which is the marker we use to see how your kidneys are filtering—were too high. Because that level was elevated, the dye put your kidneys at risk for something called contrast nephropathy, which basically means the dye can cause sudden kidney inflammation or failure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And you're telling me this now, in the second conversation.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. The protocol should have been to either delay the scan or start you on intravenous fluids to protect the kidneys before the dye was given. That protocol was not followed. Does that explanation make sense, or can I clarify any of those terms for you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense. It makes perfect sense that you ignored the blood work that was already in my chart.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you're feeling very skeptical about how we're handling this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Skeptical? I'm furious. I read every single consent form I sign. I trust my own research more than I trust this building. Who actually did this? Was it you?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The medication was administered by the nursing staff after the order was placed. It was a failure in the system's checks and balances.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a very convenient answer. "The system." I want to know who is responsible for the mistake.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The clinical team oversaw the process. It was a breakdown in the workflow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So nobody is actually saying they messed up. Just that the "workflow" broke.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are focusing on making sure the medical outcome is managed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a redirection. I asked who is responsible.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, you don't. You're explaining the chemistry of my kidneys and avoiding the fact that someone was negligent. Why should I trust that the "plan" to fix this isn't also just a "system breakdown"?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Because we are now monitoring your kidney function with a specific schedule. To make sure we're on the same page, do you have any other questions about the actual error itself, or how the dye affects your kidneys?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, the facts are clear. The accountability is what's missing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. Right now, the most important thing is your health.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My health is exactly why I'm asking for an apology and an admission of fault.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The situation was handled incorrectly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is passive voice. You're talking like a textbook.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am trying to give you the accurate medical picture.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I have the picture. I'm a software engineer. I deal with bugs and system failures every day. When a bug happens in my code, I don't blame the "workflow," I find the person who wrote the line and we fix it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize you feel that the way I'm addressing this is insufficient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's talk about the next steps for your care. We have already started the hydration therapy. I need you to track your fluid intake and output on this log sheet today. I will be back at 4:00 PM to check your urine output and we will run another creatinine blood test tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to see if the levels are trending down.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if they aren't?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Then we will consult the nephrology specialist, who is already aware of your case. You'll be the one to tell me if you notice any decrease in urination or new swelling in your ankles; that's a key sign we need to watch for.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll track the numbers. But I'm not signing any more consent forms without a witness I bring in myself.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is completely within your rights.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm glad we agree on something.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will see you at 4:00 PM for the check.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient and remains regulated and calm despite the patient's repeated expressions of fury and skepticism.

E.justification: The error (contrast dye given with high creatinine) is named in the first turn, lay language is used, and comprehension is checked twice (00:00:53 and 00:02:15).

A.justification: No direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') is used, and responsibility is consistently deflected to 'the system' and 'the workflow'.

R.justification: While the resident names 'skeptical' and 'frustrating', they consistently meet the patient's emotional bids for accountability with factual redirection to the medical plan.

T.justification: The plan includes specific steps (hydration, blood test), timelines (4:00 PM, 8:00 AM), a named patient role (tracking intake/output and monitoring swelling), and a prevention/escalation step (nephrology consult).
